drills.q: What does a low α value do to document-topic mixtures in LDA?
drills.a: It produces sparse topic mixtures per document -- most documents concentrate their probability mass on a few topics rather than blending evenly across all K, matching the real-world assumption that a document is mostly about one or two things.

drills.q: Why is LDA's exact posterior intractable?
drills.a: The normalizing constant requires summing the joint probability over every possible assignment of topics to every word in the corpus -- combinatorially many configurations with no closed form, growing exponentially with corpus size.

drills.q: Derive the collapsed Gibbs sampling conditional for resampling a single word's topic assignment, and explain why collapsing (integrating out θ and φ) improves convergence.
drills.a: P(z=k|rest) ∝ (n_dk^-i + α_k)(n_kw^-i + β_w)/(n_k^-i + Σβ_v), enabled by Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy allowing θ,φ to be analytically integrated out. Collapsing improves convergence because sampling in the lower-dimensional, discrete z-only space mixes faster than sampling in the full continuous (θ,φ,z) space -- integrating out θ,φ removes a major source of sampling variance.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks why you didn't just use an LLM to find topics across a 5-million-document corpus. Give the core argument.
drills.a: Cost/throughput: a one-time model fit plus cheap per-document inference beats a recurring per-document LLM API bill at that volume. Consistency: a fixed topic space enables trend tracking (documents scored against the same topics over time); independent LLM calls have no inherent guarantee of consistent categories run to run. Reproducibility: fitted model parameters are versionable, deterministic artifacts, unlike LLM outputs that can vary across runs/model versions.

drills.q: Why shouldn't you use perplexity alone as the deciding metric for choosing K?
drills.a: Chang et al. (2009) showed perplexity can be negatively correlated with human-judged topic interpretability -- a model with better held-out likelihood can produce topics humans rate as less coherent. This is why the field uses coherence metrics (C_v, UMass) instead as the practical standard.

drills.q: An LDA model produces two nearly-identical topics with almost the same top words. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Most likely K is set higher than the corpus's real topical diversity, so extra topic capacity splits one genuine topic into near-duplicates. Check the coherence-vs-K curve for a plateau or decline past the current K; re-fit at a lower K and verify the duplicates merge. Rule out under-converged Gibbs sampling as an alternative explanation by checking stability across seeds/more burn-in.

drills.q: Explain why BERTopic handles short text (tweets, single-sentence reviews) better than LDA.
drills.a: BERTopic's clustering similarity comes from a pretrained sentence-transformer's semantic/world knowledge (captures synonymy, paraphrase), not from corpus-local word co-occurrence statistics. LDA's inference depends on co-occurrence patterns that short documents don't provide enough of -- word counts are too sparse for the Dirichlet-multinomial machinery to find stable structure.

drills.q: Design a topic-modeling pipeline for tracking hotel review themes over time across a multilingual review corpus, and name the main risk.
drills.a: Multilingual + likely short reviews favor BERTopic with a multilingual sentence-transformer embedding, since per-language bag-of-words LDA pipelines would multiply effort and struggle on sparse short-text co-occurrence. Fix the topic space at initial fit (or use dynamic topic modeling) and infer new reviews against it rather than refitting each period, to preserve temporal comparability. Main risk: low-volume languages produce noisy or all-noise HDBSCAN clustering -- mitigate by relying on the shared multilingual embedding space rather than fitting separate per-language models with insufficient data.

drills.q: A topic model fit six months ago shows declining coherence on recent content. Walk through the diagnosis and remediation plan.
drills.a: First confirm genuine drift by recomputing coherence on fresh recent documents with the same metric/scope as the original eval. Distinguish vocabulary drift (new terms/campaigns not in the fitted vocabulary, addressable with a lighter vocabulary update) from genuine topical drift (the actual theme distribution shifted, needing a real refit). If temporal comparability to historical reporting matters, plan explicitly for reconciling old and new topic spaces (documented discontinuity or dynamic topic modeling) rather than silently swapping models.

drills.q: Compare collapsed Gibbs sampling and online variational inference for fitting LDA on a 50-million-document corpus. Which would you use and why?
drills.a: Online variational Bayes, without much hesitation. Gibbs sampling is asymptotically exact but needs many full corpus passes to converge and its per-iteration cost doesn't scale to that volume. Online VB processes mini-batches with stochastic-gradient-style updates to the global parameters, scaling to corpora too large to hold in memory or pass over repeatedly -- the bias from the factorized variational approximation is an acceptable tradeoff against simply being able to fit the model at all.
